claims.source: Using previously validated RNAi constructs (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014; Llauró et al., 2018; Marcianò et al., 2021), we found that knockdown of KKT7 or KKT9 resulted in dispersal of YFP-Aurora BAUK1 from kinetochores in ~70% of cells (Figure 4A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claims.claim: Depletion of KKT1, KKT2, KKT3, KKT4, KKT6, KKT10/19, KKT14, and KKT16 had little or no effect on YFP-Aurora BAUK1 localization
claims.source: In contrast, depletion of KKT1, KKT2, KKT3, KKT4, KKT6, KKT10/19, KKT14, and KKT16 had little or no effect on YFP-Aurora BAUK1 localization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Expression of GFP-KKT72-261-LacI or GFP-KKT8-LacI resulted in robust recruitment of tdTomato-Aurora BAUK1 to LacO foci in S phase
claims.source: Expression of GFP-KKT72-261-LacI or GFP-KKT8-LacI resulted in robust recruitment of tdTomato-Aurora BAUK1 to LacO foci in S phase (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Ectopically expressed GFP-KKT8-LacI remained at kinetochores during anaphase
claims.source: Intriguingly, we also noticed that, unlike endogenous KKT8 (which is not present in anaphase), ectopically expressed GFP-KKT8-LacI remained at kinetochores during anaphase (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: AF2 confidently predicted coiled coils between KKT8 and KKT12 and between KKT9 and KKT11
claims.source: AF2 confidently predicted coiled coils between KKT8 and KKT12 and between KKT9 and KKT11 (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H), suggesting that KKT8:KKT12 and KKT9:KKT11 each form distinct subcomplexes.
claims.evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 predictions shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H.

claims.claim: 6HIS-KKT8 efficiently pulled down KKT9, KKT11, and KKT12
claims.source: 6HIS-KKT8 efficiently pulled down KKT9, KKT11, and KKT12, as shown previously (Ishii and Akiyoshi, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein purification data shown in Figure 4I and a citation to Ishii and Akiyoshi, 2020.

claims.claim: KKT12 is required for the formation of the full KKT8 complex
claims.source: In contrast, 6HIS-KKT8 could not be recovered without KKT12, indicating that KKT12 is required for the formation of the full KKT8 complex.
claims.evidence: This is based on protein purification data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: ~70% of crosslinks were compatible with the KKT7-KKT8 complex model using a distance cut-off of 30 Å
claims.source: Using a distance cut-off of 30 Å, ~70% of crosslinks were compatible with the model (Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of IP-CLMS data with the AF2 model shown in Figure 4G and H.

claims.claim: Knockdown of any subunit of the KKT8 complex affected protein levels and kinetochore localization of the other subunits
claims.source: We found that knockdown of any subunit of the KKT8 complex affected protein levels and kinetochore localization of the other subunits, indicating that presence of all subunits is required to stabilize the full complex.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: AF2 predicted with high confidence interactions between KKT9:KKT11 and a conserved region (residues ~722–741) within the KIN-A C-terminal tail
claims.source: Intriguingly, AF2 predicted with high confidence interactions between KKT9:KKT11 and a conserved region (residues ~722–741) within the KIN-A C-terminal tail, which we termed conserved domain 1 (CD1) (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 predictions shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: CD1 and CD2 synergistically promote kinetochore localization of KIN-A
claims.source: These data suggest that CD1 and CD2 synergistically promote kinetochore localization of KIN-A, with CD1 interacting with KKT9:KKT11 and CD2 possibly interacting with another receptor at the kinetochore.
claims.evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data of domain deletion constructs shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-F.

claims.claim: Deletion of CD1 severely weakens the affinity of KIN-A for kinetochores and shifts the balance toward microtubule binding
claims.source: KIN-A∆CD1-YFP was detectable at kinetochores in G2 but predominantly localized to the mitotic spindle from (pro)metaphase onward (Figure 5D and F), indicating that removal of CD1 severely weakens the affinity of KIN-A for kinetochores and instead shifts the balance toward microtubule binding.
claims.evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5D and F.

claims.claim: Despite a substantial loss of Aurora BAUK1 from kinetochores in metaphase, ∆CD1 cells exhibited normal cell cycle profiles
claims.source: Remarkably, despite a substantial loss of Aurora BAUK1 from kinetochores in metaphase, ∆CD1 cells exhibited normal cell cycle profiles (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H) and showed only a modest decrease in proliferation rates (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell cycle profile data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H and growth curve data in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: KIN-B is unlikely to be a functional kinesin based on the absence of several well-conserved residues and motifs within the motor domain
claims.source: KIN-B is unlikely to be a functional kinesin based on the absence of several well-conserved residues and motifs within the motor domain, which are fully present in KIN-A (Li et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and a citation to Li et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The motor domain of KIN-B failed to localize to the mitotic spindle when expressed ectopically
claims.source: Consistent with this, the motor domain of KIN-B, contrary to KIN-A, failed to localize to the mitotic spindle when expressed ectopically (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and did not co-sediment with microtubules in our in vitro assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and microtubule co-sedimentation assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The rigor mutation did not affect recruitment of KIN-A to kinetochores
claims.source: The rigor mutation did not affect recruitment of KIN-A to kinetochores (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: ATPase activity of KIN-A promotes chromosome congression to the metaphase plate
claims.source: However, KIN-AG210A-YFP-marked kinetochores were misaligned in ~50% of cells arrested in metaphase, suggesting that ATPase activity of KIN-A promotes chromosome congression to the metaphase plate (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-G.

claims.claim: The KIN-A rigor mutant failed to concentrate at the central spindle in anaphase
claims.source: In anaphase, the KIN-A rigor mutant failed to concentrate at the central spindle and instead widely decorated the mitotic spindle, with increased signal observed at spindle poles likely due to poleward flux (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claims.claim: Expression of the KIN-AG210A rigor mutant prevented Aurora BAUK1 from translocating to the central spindle and caused lagging chromosomes
claims.source: Importantly, expression of the KIN-AG210A rigor mutant prevented Aurora BAUK1 from translocating to the central spindle and caused lagging chromosomes (Figure 6D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claims.claim: The KIN-A rigor mutation slowed cell proliferation and caused accumulation of cells in anaphase
claims.source: The KIN-A rigor mutation also slowed cell proliferation even in the presence of wild-type protein and caused accumulation of cells in anaphase (Figure 6G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6G and cell cycle profile data in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: Central spindle localization of the CPC depends on KIN-A's ATPase activity
claims.source: We conclude that central spindle localization of the CPC depends on KIN-A's ATPase activity and is required for proper chromosome segregation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the KIN-A rigor mutant experiments.

claims.claim: The trypanosome CPC is a pentameric complex comprising Aurora BAUK1, INCENPCPC1, CPC2, KIN-A, and KIN-B
claims.source: Here, by combining biochemical, structural, and cell biological approaches in procyclic form T. brucei, we show that the trypanosome CPC is a pentameric complex comprising Aurora BAUK1, INCENPCPC1, CPC2, and the two orphan kinesins KIN-A and KIN-B.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a main finding of the study.

claims.claim: The KKT7-KKT8 complex pathway serves as the main CPC recruitment arm in trypanosomes
claims.source: Furthermore, we identify the KKT7-KKT8 complex pathway as the main kinetochore recruitment arm of the trypanosome CPC.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a main finding of the study.

claims.claim: The KIN-A:KIN-B subcomplex represents the localization module of the trypanosome CPC
claims.source: Thus, the KIN-A:KIN-B subcomplex represents the localization module of the trypanosome CPC.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Kinesins may have served as the original transport vehicles for Aurora kinases in early eukaryotes
claims.source: Our findings highlight the evolutionary diversity of CPC proteins and raise the possibility that kinesins may have served as the original transport vehicles for Aurora kinases in early eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement in the abstract based on the findings.

results.result: KIN-A and KIN-B are bona fide CPC proteins in T. brucei that form a scaffold for CPC assembly and exhibit dynamic localization throughout the cell cycle, localizing to kinetochores from S phase to metaphase, then translocating to the central spindle in anaphase, with an additional population at the new FAZ tip from late anaphase onward.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 provide strong biochemical (IP-MS) and cell biological (fluorescence microscopy) evidence that KIN-A and KIN-B are integral CPC components with dynamic localization patterns. The reciprocal IP-MS experiments (C24, C25) and colocalization studies (C26-C28) convincingly demonstrate that these kinesins are constitutive CPC members, supporting the main conclusions (C1, C2, C70, C72).

results.result: KIN-A and KIN-B are required for kinetochore localization of Aurora BAUK1 and INCENPCPC1, with KIN-A and KIN-B mutually dependent on each other for localization and stability. The central coiled-coil domain and C-terminal disordered tail of KIN-A are both required for kinetochore localization of the CPC.
results.evaluation: The RNAi depletion experiments (C33-C37) systematically demonstrate the hierarchical dependencies within the CPC, showing that KIN-A and KIN-B are upstream of Aurora BAUK1 and INCENPCPC1 localization. The Western blot data (C38) and domain deletion experiments (C39) provide additional mechanistic insights. The experimental design is rigorous with appropriate controls.

results.result: Structural modeling using AlphaFold2 combined with IP-CLMS validation reveals that KIN-A and KIN-B form parallel coiled coils that serve as a scaffold for CPC assembly, with INCENPCPC1 and CPC2 N-terminal domains interacting with the KIN-A:KIN-B coiled coils, and Aurora BAUK1 forming the catalytic module with the INCENPCPC1 C-terminus.
results.evaluation: The combination of computational predictions (C40-C43) with experimental validation via IP-CLMS (C44-C48) provides strong structural evidence. The ~85% compatibility of crosslinks with the AF2 model (C48) is excellent validation. However, the authors appropriately note that some violated crosslinks may reflect conformational flexibility, which is a reasonable interpretation.

results.result: The KKT7-KKT8 complex pathway serves as the main kinetochore recruitment arm for the CPC in trypanosomes, with KKT7 and KKT9 knockdown causing dispersal of Aurora BAUK1 from kinetochores in ~70% of cells, while ectopic recruitment experiments demonstrate that KKT7 and KKT8 are sufficient to recruit Aurora BAUK1 to ectopic loci.
results.evaluation: The RNAi screen (C49, C50) systematically identifies KKT7 and KKT9 as critical for CPC recruitment, while the LacI-LacO tethering experiments (C51, C52) provide strong gain-of-function evidence. The observation that ectopic KKT8 traps Aurora BAUK1 at kinetochores during anaphase (C52) provides additional mechanistic insight into the regulation of CPC dynamics.

results.result: The KKT8 complex consists of two subcomplexes, KKT8:KKT12 and KKT9:KKT11, with KKT12 required for formation of the full complex. AlphaFold2 predictions are supported by ~70% compatibility with IP-CLMS crosslinks and biochemical reconstitution experiments.
results.evaluation: The structural predictions (C53) are well-validated by both biochemical reconstitution in E. coli (C54, C55) and IP-CLMS data (C56). The interdependency experiments (C57) provide additional support for the model. The combination of computational, biochemical, and cell biological approaches provides strong converging evidence.

results.result: The C-terminal tail of KIN-A contains two conserved domains (CD1 and CD2) that synergistically promote kinetochore localization, with CD1 (residues ~722-741) interacting with KKT9:KKT11. Deletion of CD1 severely weakens kinetochore affinity and shifts localization toward microtubule binding, yet cells exhibit only modest growth defects.
results.evaluation: The AlphaFold2 predictions (C58) combined with domain deletion experiments (C59, C60) provide strong evidence for the role of CD1 and CD2. The observation that ΔCD1 cells show normal cell cycle profiles despite substantial loss of Aurora BAUK1 from kinetochores (C61) is surprising but well-documented, paralleling findings in budding yeast as the authors note.

results.result: The N-terminal motor domain of KIN-A promotes CPC translocation to spindle microtubules in anaphase through its ATPase activity. KIN-B is likely a non-functional kinesin. The KIN-A rigor mutant (G210A) fails to concentrate at the central spindle, prevents Aurora BAUK1 translocation, causes lagging chromosomes, and leads to cell cycle defects.
results.evaluation: The sequence analysis and functional experiments (C62, C63) convincingly demonstrate that KIN-B lacks motor activity. The rigor mutant experiments (C64-C69) provide strong evidence that KIN-A motor activity is required for central spindle localization and proper chromosome segregation. The phenotypic characterization is thorough, including localization, growth, and cell cycle analyses.

results.result: Bioinformatic analysis reveals that KIN-A and KIN-B are present in trypanosomatids and bodonids, with KIN-A detectable in prokinetoplastids. CPC2 is restricted to trypanosomatids, while Aurora BAUK1 and INCENPCPC1 are present across kinetoplastids, diplonemids, and euglenids. Borealin, Survivin, KIN-A, and KIN-B are absent from diplonemids and euglenids.
results.evaluation: The bioinformatic analysis (C29-C32) is appropriately conducted using reciprocal BLAST searches and provides important evolutionary context. The methods section describes the approach adequately. The speculation about non-canonical CPC proteins in diplonemids and euglenids (C32) is reasonable given the data but appropriately presented as speculation.

results.result: Background claims establishing the known biology of Aurora B kinase, CPC composition and function in model eukaryotes, CPC recruitment pathways in vertebrates, and the unique kinetochore proteins in kinetoplastids.
results.evaluation: These claims (C7-C23) represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. They provide necessary context for understanding the novelty of the current work. The citations appear appropriate and the claims accurately represent prior work.

results.result: The findings raise the possibility that kinesins may have served as the original transport vehicles for Aurora kinases in early eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: This evolutionary speculation (C73) is interesting but not directly tested in the manuscript. While the discovery of kinesin-based CPC localization in kinetoplastids is novel and the evolutionary analysis shows conservation patterns, the claim about ancestral function requires additional phylogenetic analysis and functional studies in other divergent eukaryotes to be substantiated.

results.result: KIN-A and KIN-B are bona fide CPC proteins that co-immunoprecipitate with Aurora B and INCENP, and display dynamic localization from kinetochores (S phase to metaphase) to the central spindle (anaphase) and FAZ tip (late anaphase onward).
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'reveals that two orphan kinesin-like proteins KIN-A and KIN-B act as localization modules of the CPC' and notes the IP-MS and localization data support this. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'demonstrate for the first time that KIN-A and KIN-B display a dynamic localisation pattern similar to other components of the CPC, providing compelling evidence for KIN-A and KIN-B being bona fide CPC proteins.' The editor calls this identification 'a clear advancement over earlier work.'

results.result: KIN-A and KIN-B form a scaffold for CPC assembly, with hierarchical dependencies showing that depletion of KIN-A or KIN-B delocalizes Aurora B and INCENP, while Aurora B depletion does not affect KIN-A/KIN-B localization. The central coiled-coil domain and C-terminal tail of KIN-A are required for kinetochore localization.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'The major conclusion is collectively supported by multiple approaches' including 'epistasis analysis of cellular localization.' Reviewer 3 notes 'They then demonstrate, by using RNAi to deplete individual components, that the CPC proteins have hierarchical interdependencies for their localisation to the kinetochores at metaphase. These experiments appear to have been well performed.' The domain deletion experiments are also described as providing 'compelling evidence.'

results.result: AlphaFold2 predictions and IP-CLMS data reveal the structural architecture of the CPC: KIN-A and KIN-B form parallel coiled coils, INCENP and CPC2 N-termini interact with these coiled coils, and ~85% of crosslinks are compatible with the AF2 model.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 emphasizes that 'IP-CLMS, AlphaFold2 structural predictions, and domain deletion analysis support' the structural model. Reviewer 3 states 'These data are strengthened by immunoprecipitating CPC complexes and crosslinking them prior to mass spectrometry analysis (IP-CLMS), a state-of-the-art approach' and notes 'Altogether these data provide compelling evidence of the protein domains required for CPC kinetochore localisation and CPC protein interactions.' The editor highlights the study is 'supported by compelling...immunoprecipitations with crosslinking/mass spec, and AlphaFold interaction predictions.'

results.result: The KKT7-KKT8 complex (comprising KKT7, KKT8, KKT9, KKT11, KKT12) serves as the main kinetochore receptor for CPC recruitment. Knockdown of KKT7 or KKT9 disperses Aurora B from kinetochores in ~70% of cells, while other KKT proteins have little effect. KKT7 and KKT8 can recruit Aurora B to ectopic loci.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'the authors show that kinetochore proteins KKT7 and KKT9 are required for AUK1 to localise to kinetochores' and 'This leads to the conclusion that the KKT8 complex is likely the main kinetochore receptor of the CPC.' Reviewer 1 notes the data support that 'the KKT7-KKT8 complex are required for CPC localization at the centromere.' The RNAi and LacI-LacO recruitment experiments are described as well-performed and convincing.

results.result: Within the KKT8 complex, KKT8:KKT12 and KKT9:KKT11 form distinct subcomplexes. All four subunits are required for complex stability, and ~70% of IP-CLMS crosslinks are compatible with the AF2 structural model.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'In general, these data are of high quality and convincing' and notes the authors 'assess the interdependencies between KKT8 complex components for localisation and expression, showing that all four subunits are required for the assembly of a stable KKT8 complex and present AlphaFold2 structural modelling data to support the two subcomplex model.' Reviewer 1 highlights 'biochemical reconstitution (the complex of KKT8, KKT9, KKT11 and KKT12)' as supporting the conclusions.

results.result: The C-terminal tail of KIN-A contains conserved domains CD1 and CD2 that interact with the KKT8 complex (specifically KKT9:KKT11 via CD1) and synergistically promote kinetochore localization. Deletion of CD1 shifts KIN-A localization toward microtubules but causes only modest growth defects.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'The authors also convincingly show that AlphaFold2 predictions of interactions between KKT9:KKT11 and a conserved domain (CD1) in the C-terminal tail of KIN-A are correct, with CD1 and a second conserved domain, CD2, identified through sequence analysis, acting synergistically to promote KIN-A kinetochore localisation at metaphase.' Reviewer 1 notes the data support that 'conserved KIN-A C-terminal CD1 and CD2 interact with the heterodimeric KKT9-KKT11 complex.'

results.result: The N-terminal motor domain of KIN-A (but not KIN-B, which is predicted to be inactive) promotes CPC translocation to spindle microtubules. A KIN-A rigor mutant (G210A) localizes to kinetochores but fails to concentrate at the central spindle in anaphase, causes chromosome misalignment, lagging chromosomes, and cell cycle defects, indicating that KIN-A ATPase activity is required for central spindle localization and proper chromosome segregation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a significant concern: 'While these data are highly suggestive that KIN-A possesses ATPase activity, and that this activity is essential for its function, definitive biochemical evidence of KIN-A's ATPase activity is still lacking.' Reviewer 1 notes a 'Minor weakness' regarding the microtubule pelleting assay interpretation due to 'substantial insoluble fractions.' While the functional data are described as 'highly suggestive,' the lack of direct biochemical evidence for ATPase activity creates uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Bioinformatic analysis reveals that KIN-A and KIN-B are present in trypanosomatids and bodonids (with KIN-A extending to prokinetoplastids), while CPC2 is trypanosomatid-specific. Aurora B and INCENP are present across kinetoplastids, diplonemids, and euglenids, but Borealin, Survivin, KIN-A, and KIN-B homologs are absent in diplonemids and euglenids.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'The evolutionary perspective makes the paper potentially interesting for a wide audience of cell biologists' and suggests the evolutionary analysis could be strengthened by extending predictions beyond T. brucei. The bioinformatic findings are not challenged but are seen as supporting the evolutionary significance of the work. The editor emphasizes the findings 'will be of interest to...those interested in the evolution of mitotic mechanisms.'

results.result: Depletion of Aurora B, INCENP, KIN-A, or KIN-B results in prominent growth defects and G2/M arrest.
results.evaluation: This finding is mentioned by reviewers as consistent with previous work (Li et al., 2008) and is not questioned. It serves as supporting evidence for the functional importance of these proteins but is treated as confirmatory rather than novel.

results.result: The trypanosome CPC is a pentameric complex comprising Aurora B, INCENP, CPC2, KIN-A, and KIN-B.
results.evaluation: This is the central conclusion of the paper and is explicitly supported by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 states 'the study reveals novel pathways of CPC localization regulation via KIN-A and KIN-B by multiple complementary approaches.' Reviewer 3 notes the work 'shed[s] light on the composition of the unusual trypanosome CPC.' The editor calls this an 'important study' that 'identifies the mitotic localization mechanism for Aurora B and INCENP.'

results.result: The KIN-A:KIN-B complex constitutes a unique 'two-in-one' CPC localization module that directs the CPC to kinetochores from S phase to metaphase and to the central spindle in anaphase.
results.evaluation: This integrative conclusion is supported by the reviewers' acceptance of the individual localization findings. Reviewer 1 notes the data support that 'KIN-A and KIN-B act as localization modules of the CPC.' Reviewer 3 states the work provides 'compelling evidence' for the dynamic localization pattern. The 'two-in-one' characterization is not explicitly challenged.

results.result: Kinesins may have served as the original transport vehicles for Aurora kinases in early eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: This speculative evolutionary claim is not directly challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 2 suggests the evolutionary perspective could be strengthened with additional structural predictions across species, but does not dispute the possibility. The editor highlights the evolutionary significance as a key strength of the paper.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on structural modeling claims (C40-C48). Both evaluations find the combination of AlphaFold2 predictions and IP-CLMS validation compelling, with ~85% crosslink compatibility providing strong structural evidence. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Complete agreement on KKT7/KKT9 and KKT8 complex findings (C49-C52, C71). Both evaluations find the RNAi screen and LacI-LacO tethering experiments convincing evidence for CPC recruitment mechanisms. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Full agreement on KKT8 complex structural and biochemical characterization (C53-C57). Both evaluations praise the combination of structural predictions, E. coli reconstitution, IP-CLMS data, and interdependency experiments. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on evolutionary/bioinformatic analysis (C29-C32). Both find the reciprocal BLAST searches and evolutionary context appropriate, though peer review suggests it could be strengthened with additional predictions. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Disagreement on evolutionary speculation (C73). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the claim requires additional phylogenetic analysis and functional studies in other eukaryotes. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, with no direct challenge to the speculation and emphasis on evolutionary significance as a strength.

Disagreement on KIN-A motor activity claims (C4, C62-C69). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the rigor mutant experiments provide strong evidence. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, noting that while data are 'highly suggestive,' definitive biochemical evidence of ATPase activity is lacking.

Agreement on CD1/CD2 domain findings (C58-C61), though peer R6 also includes C3. Both evaluations find the AlphaFold2 predictions combined with domain deletion experiments convincing. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on KIN-A/KIN-B as CPC components (C1, C24-C28). Both evaluations find IP-MS and colocalization data compelling. OpenEval R1 includes additional claims (C2, C70, C72, C25, C26, C27, C28) while peer R1 focuses on core identification. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on hierarchical dependencies within CPC (C34-C39). OpenEval R2 includes C33 while peer R2 includes C2 and C72. Both find RNAi depletion experiments and domain deletions rigorous and convincing. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Overlap on C33 (RNAi depletion causing growth defects). OpenEval R2 includes this as part of broader hierarchical dependency analysis (SUPPORTED). Peer R9 treats it as confirmatory of previous work rather than novel, but still SUPPORTED.

Overlap on C70 (novel CPC localization pathways). OpenEval R1 includes C70 as part of broader evidence for KIN-A/KIN-B as CPC components. Peer R10 treats this as the central conclusion of the paper. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Overlap on C2 and C72 (hierarchical organization and localization regulation). OpenEval R1 groups these with KIN-A/KIN-B identification claims. Peer R2 focuses on epistasis analysis and RNAi experiments. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Minimal overlap on C6 (central spindle localization). OpenEval R7 includes C6 as part of motor activity analysis. Peer R11 addresses C5 and C6 as integrative conclusion about 'two-in-one' localization modules. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R9 addresses background/literature claims (C7-C23) as appropriately cited established knowledge (SUPPORTED). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as these are contextual rather than novel findings.
